title: Pipkin and the Sunny Hill Bell
markdown:
A long time ago, when the flowers still hummed to the bees, there lived a little mouse named Pipkin. His whiskers wiggled with every puff of air. His eyes were shiny buttons, always looking for something new. He had a snug home under the roots of a big old oak, right at the bottom of Sunny Hill.

Sunny Hill was not a mountain that poked the clouds. It was a soft round hill, like a green pillow for the sky, covered in short grass and cheerful yellow flowers that looked like little suns.

At the very tip-top, where the sunbeams loved to play, sat a tiny bell. Shiny brass, no bigger than Pipkin’s paw. Wind and rain had polished it bright. From his home it was just a twinkle against the blue. He dreamed of its clear happy sound, a sweet song for all the meadow.

“Oh, how I wish I could ring that bell,” he would whisper, his small chest puffing with a brave thought.

But Pipkin was just a little mouse. Sunny Hill, even though it looked friendly, was a long way for tiny legs. Once, when he was even smaller, he had tried. The grass blades were taller than he was. The gentle breeze felt like a giant breath that could blow him over. The hill had felt too, too big.

One bright morning Pipkin sat near a daisy, drawing his wish in the soft dirt with a stick. A large kind shadow fell over him. Daisy the donkey. She was as gentle as a warm hug, with long ears that drooped with kindness and a heart as big as her strong legs. She had a quiet comforting way, and she loved to see her friends’ faces shining.

“Good morning, Pipkin,” she said, her voice a soft friendly sound, like faraway thunder. She lowered her head. Her big kind eyes met his.

Pipkin’s nose wiggled. “Oh, Daisy. Good morning. I was just wishing. Wishing so much that I could ring the little brass bell on top of Sunny Hill.” He sighed, a tiny puff of mouse breath.

Daisy tilted her head. Her long ears turned. She looked up the hill. It did look quite far.

“That sounds like a lovely wish. It’s a long way up, isn’t it?”

“Oh yes.” Pipkin’s voice went a little higher. “The grass is so tall, and the wind feels like a big puff that pushes me back. Very strong for a little mouse.” He gave a tiny shiver, just thinking how big the hill seemed.

Daisy bent down slowly, her long legs folding. “Tell you what. Why don’t you climb onto my back? You can sit right near my ears, where the wind can’t tickle you. I’ll carry you all the way to the top. We can climb Sunny Hill together.”

Pipkin’s eyes sparkled like raindrops in the sun. “Would you really? That would be so wonderful.”

“Of course,” Daisy said, her nose wrinkling a little.

So, with a jump and a scramble, Pipkin climbed her strong leg and settled between her long soft ears. It felt like the warmest pillow. The world already looked different. Daisy gave a gentle push with her back legs and began to walk, steady and soft. Up, up, up. The meadow spread below them, a green and yellow quilt. The field mice houses looked like tiny pebbles.

“Look, Daisy.” Pipkin pointed with a tiny paw. “See the little red bug with black dots? A tiny jewel. And the stream. A shiny silver ribbon.”

Daisy’s eyes crinkled. “You have such sharp eyes. Keep pointing out the lovely things. This hill has so many wonders.”

The walk was slow and peaceful. Daisy’s hooves made a soft thud on the grass, a gentle beat that made Pipkin feel safe. He felt bigger and braver than he ever had, sitting high. He pointed out a bright blue flower the color of the sky, and a fluffy white cloud that looked like a sheep.

Higher up, the grass grew taller and tickled Daisy’s long nose. And when Daisy’s nose got tickled, well.

“Ah. Ah. Achoo!”

A big happy sneeze. Not loud or startling. A rumbling one that made her ears wiggle. The sneeze tickled Pipkin. He tried to be still. He could not. He giggled, a tiny bubbly sound that tumbled out like little bells. Daisy sneezed again, softer. Pipkin giggled more, wobbling between her ears, holding on tight.

“Oh my,” Daisy chuckled, eyes a little watery. “That grass is very wiggly today. It seems to be telling jokes.”

Just after the tickly grass and the happy giggles, Pipkin looked up, heart beating fast.

“Daisy. I can see it. The bell. Right there. We’re almost there.”

They reached the top. The little brass bell gleamed, prettier than he had imagined. He slid down Daisy’s warm neck, paws finding their footing, and stood on tiptoe, reaching with all his might. He stretched his tiny body as tall as it could be. His paws still could not quite reach the little brass hammer inside the bell.

Daisy nudged him with her soft nose. “A little higher. You’re so close.”

She lowered her head, bringing her ears closer to the ground. Pipkin scrambled onto one ear and held on as she dipped. Then, with a hop and a brave jump, he reached the bell. He pushed the little brass hammer with all his might.

Ding.

The sound was clear and sweet. Not loud. A happy little tune on the breeze. The most beautiful sound Pipkin had ever heard. He hopped up and down.

“I did it. I really did it. I rang the bell.”

Daisy let out a soft happy bray. They looked out at the meadow, warm sunshine on their faces. Pipkin did not make a speech about bravery. He only sat on Daisy’s ear a little longer, the ding still living in the air, and watched the yellow flowers below look a little more like suns now that he had been to the place they pointed at.
